title: Fatigue in long efforts
goal: Explain how glycogen depletion, low blood glucose, heat and fluid loss cause fatigue in efforts of hours, and how this shows up as durability.

steps.title: The wall: running out of glycogen
steps.text:
Muscles hold about 400 g of [glycogen](g:glycogen) and the liver about 80–100 g. In long, hard efforts, running both down is a major cause of fatigue, and more glycogen at the start means more endurance [[c:glycogen-fatigue]]. Runners call the sudden late slowdown this can bring *hitting the wall*.

Why would low glycogen weaken a muscle, not just slow its fuel supply? Part of the answer is local. In human muscle, low glycogen goes with impaired Ca²⁺ release from the SR, the same link that fails in *Peripheral fatigue* [[c:glycogen-ca]]. This may be a signal that stops the muscle from draining its last energy store.

claims.text: Glycogen depletion in muscle and liver is a major cause of fatigue in endurance and high-intensity intermittent exercise; high-carbohydrate diets raise muscle glycogen and improve exercise capacity.

evidence.quote: glycogen depletion (in both muscle and liver) is a major cause of fatigue in both endurance and high-intensity (intermittent) type activities.
high CHO diets increase muscle glycogen storage and subsequently improve exercise capacity

claims.text: In human muscle, low glycogen is associated with impaired SR Ca²⁺ release, which may link energy content to fatigue.

evidence.quote: We show that low muscle glycogen is associated with an impairment of muscle ability to release Ca(2+), which is an important signal in the muscle activation.

These data provide indications of a signal that links energy utilization, i.e. muscle contraction, with the energy content in the muscle, thereby inhibiting a detrimental depletion of the muscle energy store.

steps.title: Low blood glucose
steps.text:
The liver keeps blood glucose up, and the brain runs mainly on glucose. When liver glycogen runs low and nothing is eaten, blood glucose falls.

In a classic study, 7 trained cyclists rode at 71% of [VO2max](g:vo2max) until exhausted [[c:coyle-glucose]]:

| | placebo | carbohydrate drink |
|---|---|---|
| time to fatigue | 3.0 h | 4.0 h |
| blood glucose near the end | 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ | 4.2–5.2 mmol·L⁻¹ |
| muscle glycogen use, first 3 h | same | same |

The drink didn't spare muscle glycogen. It kept blood glucose up, so the riders kept burning carbohydrate from other sources for an extra hour. [Hypoglycaemia](g:hypoglycaemia), not only empty muscles, ended the placebo ride.

claims.text: In trained cyclists at 71% VO2max, fatigue at 3 h without carbohydrate followed a fall in plasma glucose to 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹; carbohydrate feeding kept glucose up and extended exercise by about 1 h without sparing muscle glycogen.

evidence.quote: Fatigue during the placebo trial occurred after 3.02 +/- 0.19 h of exercise and was preceded by a decline (P less than 0.01) in plasma glucose to 2.5 +/- 0.5 mM
The pattern of muscle glycogen utilization, however, was not different during the first 3 h of exercise with the placebo or the carbohydrate feedings.

steps.title: Heat: the drive backs off
steps.text:
*Heat and the heart* showed trained cyclists at a fixed power stopping at about the same [core temperature](g:core-temperature), near 40 °C, whatever they started at [[c:critical-temp]], and why that 'critical temperature' is debated.

What gives way? Partly the nervous system. After cycling to exhaustion in 40 °C heat, men held a 2 min maximal knee extension with voluntary activation of 54%, against 82% after riding in cool air (worked out a slightly different way from the formula in *Central fatigue*). Electrical stimulation brought total force to the same level in both [[c:heat-va]]. The muscle could still work; the drive to it had dropped.

claims.text: In uncompensable heat, trained cyclists at 60% VO2max reached exhaustion at the same core temperature (about 40 °C) regardless of starting temperature; time to exhaustion fell as starting temperature rose.

evidence.quote: Despite different initial temperatures, all subjects fatigued at an identical level of hyperthermia (Tes = 40. 1-40.2 degrees C, muscle temperature = 40.7-40.9 degrees C, skin temperature = 37.0-37.2 degrees C)
Time to exhaustion was inversely related to the initial body temperature: 63 +/- 3, 46 +/- 3, and 28 +/- 2 min with initial Tes of approximately 36, 37, and 38 degrees C, respectively

claims.text: After exhausting exercise in the heat, voluntary activation during a sustained maximal contraction was 54% versus 82% in the control trial, while total force with stimulation did not differ.

evidence.quote: Calculation of the voluntary activation percentage (MVC/MVC + EL) revealed that the degree of central activation was significantly lower in hyperthermia (54 +/- 7%) compared with control (82 +/- 6%). In contrast, total force of the knee extensors (MVC + force from EL) was not different in the two trials.

steps.title: Dehydration: the 2% rule or thirst?
steps.text:
Long efforts lose body water as sweat. The ACSM advises drinking enough to avoid losing more than 2% of body mass, to prevent a fall in performance [[c:acsm-2pct]].

A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) questioned how much this matters in racing. Across 5 cycling time-trial studies (39 riders), losing up to 4% of body mass didn't change outdoor performance; exercise intensity and duration mattered far more, and drinking to thirst did best [[c:goulet]].

That evidence is small and cycling-only, so the question is open. Both sides agree that big losses in the heat hurt, and that sweat rates vary a lot between people.

claims.text: The ACSM advises drinking during exercise to prevent excessive dehydration (more than 2% body-mass loss) and so avoid compromised performance.

evidence.quote: The goal of drinking during exercise is to prevent excessive (>2% body weight loss from water deficit) dehydration and excessive changes in electrolyte balance to avert compromised performance.

claims.text: In a meta-analysis of cycling time trials, exercise-induced dehydration of up to 4% body mass did not alter outdoor performance, and drinking to thirst performed best.

evidence.quote: Compared with euhydration, EID (up to 4% BW loss) does not alter cycling performances during out-of-door exercise conditions; (2) exercise intensity and duration have a much greater impact on cycling TT performances than EID and; (3) relying on thirst sensation to gauge the need for fluid replacement maximises cycling TT performances.

debate.question: Does losing more than 2% of body mass as sweat impair endurance performance?

sides.position: Yes: drink to prevent losses above 2% of body mass to avoid compromised performance (ACSM).
Not in self-paced outdoor cycling: up to 4% loss didn't change time-trial performance, and drinking to thirst did best (Goulet).

steps.title: Durability: when your numbers drift
steps.text:
Lab tests are done fresh. But thresholds, efficiency and power don't stay fixed over hours of exercise; they drift. Maunder and colleagues call an athlete's resistance to this [durability](g:durability): how soon, and how much, the profile worsens during prolonged exercise [[c:durability]].

Everything in this lesson feeds it: falling glycogen and blood glucose, heat, fluid loss, and central and peripheral fatigue building up.

The practical result: zones from a fresh test overestimate what you can hold in hour five, which matters for pacing long races and planning long sessions. The module *Durability: the fourth dimension* covers how to measure and train it.

claims.text: Physiological-profiling attributes change during prolonged exercise; durability is the time of onset and magnitude of their deterioration, which affects intensity regulation in long sessions and races.

evidence.quote: the attributes measured during routine physiological-profiling assessments are not static, but change over time during prolonged exercise.
here defined as the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profiling characteristics over time during prolonged exercise.

If not accounted for, shifts in these physiological attributes during prolonged exercise have implications for the accuracy of their use in intensity regulation during prolonged training sessions or competitions

points: Depleting muscle and liver glycogen is a major cause of fatigue in long efforts; low glycogen also impairs Ca²⁺ release.
Without carbohydrate, blood glucose can fall to about 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ and end a ride; feeding kept riders going an hour longer without sparing muscle glycogen.
In heat the body can't shed, fixed-power exercise ended at a core temperature near 40 °C, with a drop in voluntary activation rather than muscle failure.
Whether more than 2% body-mass loss hurts self-paced performance is debated; thirst-guided drinking did well in outdoor cycling.
Durability is how soon and how much your profile drifts in long exercise; fresh-test zones overestimate late-race capacity.

variants.stem: Trained cyclists riding to exhaustion at 71% of VO2max lasted about an hour longer when they drank carbohydrate. How did the drink help?

options.text: It kept blood glucose up as a fuel source
options.why: Right: glucose stayed at 4.2–5.2 mmol·L⁻¹ and carbohydrate oxidation was maintained.

options.text: It slowed the use of muscle glycogen
options.why: Muscle glycogen was used at the same rate in the first 3 h in both trials.

options.text: It kept the riders cooler
options.why: The study was about fuel; nothing points to a cooling effect.

options.text: It lowered their blood lactate
options.why: Lactate wasn't what ended the placebo ride.

variants.stem: In that study, what happened just before the riders on placebo had to stop?

options.text: Blood glucose fell to about 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: Right: fatigue followed a fall in plasma glucose.

options.text: Muscle glycogen use suddenly sped up
options.why: Glycogen use slowed in the final hour, to less than half its earlier rate.

options.text: Core temperature reached about 40 °C
options.why: That's the heat studies; this ride wasn't heat-limited.

options.text: Blood lactate rose sharply
options.why: At 71% of VO2max lactate stays fairly steady.

variants.stem: On a cool morning, a marathoner is on target pace at 30 km, then slows by 90 s per km over the next 3 km. He ate a light breakfast and took no gels. Most likely cause?

options.text: Muscle and liver glycogen running low
options.why: Right: a late, sharp slowdown without fuel is the classic wall.

options.text: Core temperature passing 40 °C
options.why: On a cool morning, overheating is unlikely.

options.text: Losing more than 2% of body mass as sweat
options.why: Sweat losses are small in the cool, and the slowdown is too sudden.

options.text: A rise in brain serotonin
options.why: The serotonin hypothesis lacks robust support.

variants.stem: Besides less fuel, how may low muscle glycogen weaken contraction?

options.text: It impairs Ca²⁺ release from the SR
options.why: Right: low glycogen is linked to impaired Ca²⁺ release in human muscle.

options.text: It stops action potentials reaching the muscle
options.why: Nerve signals still reach the muscle; the change is inside the fibre.

options.text: It raises blood lactate to toxic levels
options.why: Low glycogen means less glycolysis, so lactate tends to be lower.

options.text: It makes the muscle fibres stiffer
options.why: Stiffness isn't the proposed link; Ca²⁺ release is.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides at 70% of VO2max on a cool day without eating. After 3 h she feels dizzy and weak and has to stop. Most likely cause?

options.text: Low blood glucose
options.why: Right: dizziness and fatigue near 3 h without food fit hypoglycaemia.

options.text: Core temperature near 40 °C
options.why: On a cool day, heat is unlikely to be the limit.

options.text: Muscle damage from the ride
options.why: Cycling causes little damage, and damage doesn't cause dizziness.

options.text: K⁺ building up around fibres
options.why: K⁺ shifts matter in intense efforts, not a moderate 3 h ride.

variants.stem: In 32 °C humid heat, a runner slows from 10 km on in a half marathon, with core temperature near 40 °C. He is well fuelled. Most likely cause?

options.text: Hyperthermia lowering the drive to the muscles
options.why: Right: high core temperature lowers voluntary activation.

options.text: Muscle glycogen stores running out
options.why: At 10 km of a half marathon, glycogen is far from empty.

options.text: Blood glucose falling too low
options.why: He is well fuelled, and it's too early for hypoglycaemia.

options.text: Pi binding Ca²⁺ inside the SR
options.why: That's a mechanism of intense efforts, not the main problem here.

variants.stem: After riding to exhaustion in 40 °C heat, a cyclist's maximal knee extension is weak. Adding electrical stimulation brings total force to the level seen after a cool ride. Where is the main problem?

options.text: In the drive from the nervous system
options.why: Right: stimulation restored force, so the muscle could still produce it.

options.text: In the muscle's contractile machinery
options.why: With stimulation, the muscle produced normal force.

options.text: In muscle glycogen running out
options.why: Stimulation restored normal force, so the muscle had the fuel to contract.

options.text: In dehydrated fibres unable to contract
options.why: The fibres contracted normally when stimulated.

variants.stem: What does the ACSM position stand advise about drinking during exercise?

options.text: Drink to prevent losing more than 2% of body mass
options.why: Right: the stated goal is to avoid more than 2% body-mass loss.

options.text: Drink 1 L per hour, whatever the sweat rate
options.why: It recommends individual plans because sweat rates vary a lot.

options.text: Drink nothing during exercise, only after
options.why: It advises drinking during exercise.

options.text: Drink as much as possible to gain body mass
options.why: Gaining mass by over-drinking isn't the goal.

variants.stem: In a 90 min outdoor time trial at 22 °C, a rider who drinks only to thirst will lose about 2.5% of body mass. What does the evidence best support?

options.text: Drinking to thirst is reasonable in these conditions
options.why: Right: up to 4% loss didn't harm outdoor cycling time trials, and thirst did best.

options.text: She must stay under 2% or she will slow down
options.why: That's the ACSM rule, but the meta-analysis of outdoor time trials found no effect up to 4%.

options.text: She should drink as much as she can stomach
options.why: Drinking above thirst gave no clear benefit.

options.text: Fluid never matters in any conditions
options.why: In the heat with large losses, dehydration does matter.

options.text: How soon and how much your profile worsens in long exercise
options.why: Right: the time of onset and size of the drift.

options.text: How fast you recover between training sessions
options.why: That's recovery, covered in the next lesson.

options.text: Your VO2max measured in a fresh test
options.why: Fresh tests are exactly what durability goes beyond.

options.text: How rarely you get injured over a season
options.why: Durability here is physiological, not injury resistance.

variants.stem: A rider's threshold is 280 W when fresh. In a 5 h ride, a test after 3 h puts it at 255 W. How should he pace a long climb in hour 4?

options.text: At or below about 255 W, the late-ride value
options.why: Right: fresh zones overestimate late-ride capacity; use the drifted value.

options.text: At 280 W, since thresholds are fixed
options.why: Thresholds drift in long exercise; that's durability.

options.text: Above 280 W, to make up lost time
options.why: Riding above even his fresh threshold late on would bring early failure.

options.text: Ignore power: thresholds can't be measured when tired
options.why: He just measured it at 3 h; that is the useful number.
